headline: Global AI infrastructure investment showing no slowdown; investors increasingly allocating to training compute and inference capacity, with Australia able to attract foreign direct investment and build an export-oriented AI capacity market
reasoning: Keane points to continued massive capital raises in the US — citing SpaceX and others deploying tens of billions into AI infrastructure that same week — as evidence that global investor appetite for AI infrastructure is undiminished. He distinguishes between the frontier training GPU side and the inferencing/new AI chip side as distinct investment thematics. He argues Australia is a safe, attractive destination for foreign direct investment in both large-scale training data centres and inference-as-a-service, and could become a pioneer in exporting AI-generated tokens and capacity. He encourages investors to do the work to understand where value accretes in the AI stack.
quote: I think that foreign investors already understand the value of these large scale AI investments. Even this week we've seen significant capital raisings occurring in the US with SpaceX and a bunch of others putting in 10s of billions of dollars into building out more infrastructure. So I don't see that slowing down. I think investors all around the world are realising the importance of AI infrastructure and they're making it clear with their investment decisions. I think that Australia plays an important part. We'll continue to attract that foreign direct investment. We'll continue to be a safe place where both the large model lab companies as well as the true inferences of service providers can build a sustainable future. And I believe Australia can play a role not just in, in housing these big data centres for, for training of these these overseas models, but we can produce the tokens or, or the, the sort of AI capacity that can then be exported.
episode_title: Valuing AI; from a CEO who went to market

headline: ASX AI thematic splitting into two sub-sectors — GPU-as-a-service (bare-metal rental to foreign hyperscalers) versus inferencing-as-a-service (onshore value-add) — with investors still working out which they value more
reasoning: Keane identifies a bifurcation emerging in the Australian listed AI infrastructure space. GPU-as-a-service players buy thousands of GPUs and rent bare-metal capacity back to larger hyperscalers or foreign AI labs, which capture the software value-add. Inferencing-as-a-service providers run models locally and help domestic organisations build applications, retaining economic value onshore. Both approaches can offer significant value to investors, but Keane argues the market is only beginning to price the distinction. He suggests the parliamentary inquiry into AI and growing community concern about data sovereignty are catalysts that could accelerate investor differentiation between the two models.
quote: You've got the GPU as a service, which is a lovely expression our industry uses, which is where an organisation would buy thousands sometimes of these GPU, these graphics processing units, and they would then rent them. They simply renting what's called the bare metal back to a larger hyperscaler or AI lab, often a foreign entity that rents those GPUs and they run their own software on it and they take the value add from that to build into their business. On the other side, you've got the inferencing as a service. That's where SCX comes in... Now both of those ways of thinking about AI sort of GPU as a service and inferencing as a service both provide I think significant value. I think what we're just seeing is investors starting to understand more about those two different parts of the AI thematic overall and deciding what they what they value more.
episode_title: Valuing AI; from a CEO who went to market

headline: Over 70% of Australian organisations care about where AI is processed and under which jurisdiction, driving demand for onshore sovereign AI infrastructure amid growing parliamentary and regulatory scrutiny
reasoning: Keane cites proprietary research showing more than 70% of Australian organisations are concerned about where their AI is processed and under whose jurisdiction. The ongoing parliamentary inquiry into AI is, in his view, making it clear that Australians want control over their data and intelligence. He frames this as a structural demand driver for sovereign AI infrastructure, arguing organisations need to be able to guarantee data residency, processing location, and information handling to their own stakeholders. This regulatory and cultural tailwind is distinct from the pure compute economics driving the GPU-as-a-service segment.
quote: I think the parliamentary inquiry is making it crystal clear that Australians care about what happens to their data and their intelligence. According to our research, more than 70% of Australian organisations care about where their AI is processed and under which jurisdiction it's processed. So I think Australians are waking up to the concept that AI needs to work for us, not us work for it. And that is all about ensuring that we can take advantage of these transformational benefits, but do it in a way where we are maintaining control over our information.
episode_title: Valuing AI; from a CEO who went to market

headline: AI value accretion has been the primary driver of US equity outperformance versus the ASX; without it, the gap largely disappears, making local AI exposure a strategic priority for Australian investors
reasoning: Keane observes that when you strip out the AI-driven uplift from US equity returns, US markets have not materially outperformed the ASX over recent periods. He uses this to argue that AI is the core engine of value accretion for equity investors globally, and that Australian investors seeking comparable returns need exposure to the AI thematic. This framing underpins the investor appetite SCX encountered during its IPO roadshow among both institutional and retail participants.
quote: If you think about the ASX and look at it's return over the last little while and you compare that with what's been happening in the US markets. If you take out the AI bump that has driven a lot of value accretion in the US, the overall U.S. markets haven't performed that much better than the Australian markets. And that indicates that AI is essential to value accretion for investors.
episode_title: Valuing AI; from a CEO who went to market

headline: Australia's first ASX-listed pure-play sovereign AI inferencing-as-a-service provider, differentiating from GPU-as-a-service peers by keeping value-add onshore and guaranteeing data residency
reasoning: SCX AI completed a fully underwritten $40 million IPO on the ASX in August, positioning itself as an inferencing-as-a-service provider rather than a GPU-as-a-service provider. The distinction matters because GPU-as-a-service players simply rent bare-metal compute to foreign hyperscalers or AI labs, which take the value-add offshore. SCX runs models from its own machines in Australia and helps Australian organisations build applications and agents, retaining that value-add domestically. The company does not retain customer data and can guarantee where and how data is processed, which Keane argues addresses a regulatory and customer concern cited by over 70% of Australian organisations. Keane sees inferencing-as-a-service as the source of ongoing value streaming back to shareholders, contrasting it with the heavy compute/frontier-training model exemplified by Firmus.
quote: SCX had our, you know, fully underwritten IPO launched in in August this year. And I think what we saw in talking to investors, both institutional investors and a whole bunch of of, of interested investors who are starting to understand the value of the AI ecosystem was that, look, if you think about the ASX and look at it's return over the last little while and you compare that with what's been happening in the US markets. If you take out the AI bump that has driven a lot of value accretion in the US, the overall U.S. markets haven't performed that much better than the Australian markets. And that indicates that AI is essential to value accretion for investors. And we found that certainly in our process that both institutional and I think general investors are looking for the, the AI thematic... On the other side, you've got the inferencing as a service. That's where SCX comes in. We're building the capability to keep that value add onshore to actually run the models from our machines here in Australia and help Australian organisations to build the applications and agents of the future.
episode_title: Valuing AI; from a CEO who went to market

headline: Zero-debt, equity-funded AI inference-as-a-service model positioned to deliver strong shareholder returns as practical AI capacity demand grows
reasoning: David Keane explains that SCX deliberately chose a zero-debt, equity-funded build-out because of anticipated inflationary headwinds and rising cost of capital. He argues the company's value accrues on the inferencing side — delivering practical AI capacity to applications and agents — rather than the capital-intensive frontier training side. He emphasises that SCX already has real customers and real services generating revenue, which he sees as the correct path to scale. He believes Australia can become an export-oriented AI capacity market, with SCX well-positioned to benefit from that structural trend.
quote: It was one of the reasons that SCX chose to build our business model with a 0 debt approach. You know, we saw the winds moving towards a higher inflationary environment and that can be tricky if you have a significant debt load. So we felt that building SCX with an equity funded programme supported by investors was going to be the best way to be able to return to those investors for our build out of AI. Look, I think though that there are real cases where of course that that that loads make sense. And that's a question for investors to understand their risk appetite on that. But look, you know, we believe that you can build AI viably. You can do it in a way that can deliver strong results. But it's one of the things we've been doing is you've got to be out in the market with a real service, with real customers, creating real capacity. And that's the way we think you can build, build, scale.
episode_title: Valuing AI; from a CEO who went to market
